title: Method for mapping Hg0 emissions from gold shops in artisanal and small-scale gold mining communities
author: Brown, Hasan, et al.

steps.title: Transport equipment to low‑Hg0 site
steps.instruction: Carry the MTIP, Lumex, GPS unit, and computer to an uncovered open area previously measured to have Hg0 levels below 100 ng/m³ and ensure the GPS has clear sky view for satellite lock.

steps.title: Power on MTIP and verify Hg0
steps.instruction: Turn on the MTIP, start its data collection, and confirm that the measured Hg0 concentration is below 1,000 ng/m³ before proceeding.

steps.title: Configure Lumex and RAPID parameters
steps.instruction: Set the Lumex and RAPID software to the following values: zero‑correction time = 40 s; frame time = 1 s; monitoring duration = 6–8 h (independent of actual collection time); zero check interval = every 20 min; alarm limit = 25,000 ng/m³.

steps.title: Pre‑condition Lumex On‑Stream
steps.instruction: Operate the Lumex in “On Stream” mode for 20 min before data collection and record the relative deviation, which must be less than 20 %.

steps.title: Synchronize time and connect devices
steps.instruction: Manually sync the computer clock to GPS time, have all team members sync their watches to GPS time, and connect the computer to the Lumex with the appropriate cable.

steps.title: Start data acquisition
steps.instruction: Launch RAPID software, select air‑analysis monitoring, verify all parameters, then press the play button in RAPID and start the GPS recording at approximately the same moment; record the Lumex start time.

steps.title: Attach GPS to Lumex bag
steps.instruction: Directly connect the GPS unit to the Lumex carrying bag.

steps.title: Import raw data into Excel
steps.instruction: Copy the Lumex output into an Excel worksheet tab named “Lumex” and copy the GPS time‑position output into a tab named “GPS”.

steps.title: Prepare GPS timestamps and coordinates
steps.instruction: In the GPS tab, delete the AM/PM designator from the time column, convert latitude and longitude to decimal degrees, and paste the cleaned data into a new tab called “VLOOKUP”.

steps.title: Prepare Lumex timestamps
steps.instruction: In the Lumex tab, delete the AM/PM designator from the time column, then copy the time and Hg0 concentration columns into the “VLOOKUP” tab.

steps.title: Match position to concentration
steps.instruction: Within the VLOOKUP tab, use the VLOOKUP function to find an exact match between each time‑stamped GPS position and the corresponding Hg0 concentration; copy the resulting position‑concentration pairs to a tab named “MAX”.

steps.title: Clean and sort concentration data
steps.instruction: In the MAX tab, sort the concentration column from smallest to largest, expand the selection to keep positions aligned, and delete any rows where the concentration is reported as “#N/A”.

steps.title: Calculate maximum per unique location
steps.instruction: Create a third column in the MAX tab containing only unique positions (remove duplicate latitude/longitude pairs), then apply the MAXIFS function to obtain the maximum Hg0 value for each unique position; copy these unique positions and their maximum concentrations to the “QGIS” tab.

steps.title: Create CSV for GIS
steps.instruction: In the QGIS tab, split the combined position column back into separate latitude and longitude columns while keeping them linked to the maximum concentration, then save the sheet as a .csv file ready for GIS import.

steps.title: Generate concentration map in QGIS
steps.instruction: Import the .csv file into QGIS (or another GIS platform), set the minimum concentration display to 0 ng/m³ and the maximum to the Lumex calibration upper limit of 42,307 ng/m³ (detection range 0.5–50,000 ng/m³), and render the map of Hg0 concentrations.

description: The city of Mazuko is one of the principle urban centers in Madre de Dios, Peru, an Amazonian department with widespread Hg pollution and deforestation resulting from ASGM activities [21], [22], [23], [24]. We were asked by municipal government officials in Mazuko to map the portion of the InterOceanic Highway that passes through their town to (1) identify point sources of Hg0 vapor originating from gold shops, (2) preliminarily quantify Hg0 concentrations near these shops, (3) discuss potential health ramifications of exposure to Hg0, and (4) place our findings in the context of air quality standards for mercury [25,26]. The data would ultimately be used by the government officials to address public health concerns related to elevated levels of mercury originating from gold shops and assist local efforts to move existing shops to less populated and traveled areas of the city. Data collection was conducted on June 13 and 14, 2019 over the course of seven experiments. Upon completion of each experiment, a map was generated. Depending upon weather and other external factors, the number of experiments each day varied. When analyzed using the method described here and in the video, the data provided in the supporting information produced the map in Fig. 1. This map is representative of data collected during one experiment.Fig. 1The map produced from the data provided in the supplemental information via the method reported here and in the video walk through.Fig. 1 Fig. 2 is the map generated from all data collected during the seven experiments, recording the maximum Hg0 concentration at each unique latitude and longitude. All emissions of Hg0 in the study area were traced back to gold shops purchasing and burning amalgams and sponge gold. According to current Peruvian air quality standards for total gaseous mercury (TGM), at no time during a 24-h period should Hg0 concentrations exceed 2,000 ng/m3 [25,26].
